name: Kites
line: From reading the wind to flying a kite you made yourself, and teaching two children to launch and land it.
who: Everybody; a grown-up with a child when flying
about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a grown-up is with a child whenever a kite is flying. It starts by reading the wind from a window, then making a small kite from paper, straws and thread and getting it into the air. From there you launch and land it on your own, keep it up for ten minutes, make a bigger kite from a bin bag and two sticks, and change its tail to make it fly better. It ends with you teaching two children to launch and land a kite you made. It costs nothing, and the safety rules come first: fly only in a wide open space, never near power lines, roads, railways or airports, and never in rain or thunder.

steps.test: Look out of a window and say whether today is a kite day, from what the trees, leaves and flags are doing.
steps.note: Leaves still and smoke going straight up: too little wind. Leaves and small twigs moving all the time, a flag standing out: good kite wind. Whole branches swaying, hard to walk against: too strong for a first kite. If you have a weather app, the wind speed for a small kite is roughly 10 to 25 kilometres an hour.

steps.test: Make a small sled kite from a sheet of paper, two drinking straws, tape and a long piece of thread.
how: Fold a sheet of printer paper in half and draw a shape like a house turned on its side: a wide middle and narrower ends. Cut it out and open it.
Tape a straw down each side of the middle, from top to bottom.
Put tape over each outer corner, make a small hole through it, and tie one piece of thread to both holes, about three times the width of the kite, as the bridle.
Tie your long flying thread to the middle of the bridle, and tape a paper strip to the bottom as a tail.
steps.note: Paper straws, plastic straws or two thin garden sticks all work. Cotton thread or fishing line on a piece of card to wind it on is enough for a small kite. A child can decorate and tape; a grown-up helps with the holes.

steps.test: Work out which way the wind is blowing in an open space before you launch.
steps.note: Stand still and turn slowly until you feel the wind evenly on your face, or drop a little grass and watch where it goes. For flying, stand with the wind on your back. Choose a field, a beach or a large park with no trees, power lines or roads nearby.

steps.test: Get your kite into the air and keep it up for one minute.
steps.note: With the wind at your back, let out a few metres of thread and let the wind lift the kite from your hand. If it drops, walk backwards a few steps to give it air. A helper holding the kite up a little way away and letting go makes the first flight easier.

steps.test: Launch the kite on your own, with nobody holding it for you.
steps.note: Hold the kite up by the bridle with the wind behind you, and let the wind take it as you let out thread slowly. On a light day, a few quick steps backwards help it climb. Never run towards a road or a slope while looking up.

steps.test: Land your kite on your own without it crashing.
steps.note: Wind the thread in steadily while walking towards the kite, so it comes down gently. If a gust pulls hard, let out a little thread instead of holding tight. Never grab a thread that is pulling fast; it can cut skin.

steps.test: Keep your kite flying for ten minutes without it coming down.
steps.note: When it dips, pull in a little thread; when it pulls strongly and climbs, let some out. Watch the tail: if it spins in circles, it needs a longer tail. Keep well away from other people's kites.

steps.test: Make a bigger sled kite from a bin bag, two sticks about as long as your arm, tape and strong string.
steps.note: The same shape as the paper kite, drawn about four times bigger on a cut-open bin bag. Garden canes, thin dowels or straight sticks work, and so does string from a parcel or a garden shed. A grown-up does any cutting of the sticks.

steps.test: Fly the bigger kite for five minutes, wearing gloves.
steps.note: A bigger kite pulls harder, so wear garden gloves or woolly gloves and wind the string onto a stick or a piece of wood, not round your hand. A child flies it with a grown-up holding the line too. If it lands in a tree or on anything high, leave it; a kite can be made again.

steps.test: Change one thing on the bigger kite, such as the length of the tail or the length of the bridle, and fly it again to see if it flies better.
steps.note: Change only one thing at a time, or you will not know what worked. A longer tail steadies a spinning kite; a longer or shorter bridle changes the angle the kite sits at in the wind. Say out loud what you changed and what happened.

steps.test: Let out about thirty metres of line, fly the kite at that height for ten minutes, and wind it all back in without a tangle.
steps.note: Thirty metres is about forty walking steps; tie a small knot in the line at that length before you go. Keep it much lower than aircraft could ever be, and well away from any airport; some countries set a height limit for kites, so find out yours. If the kite ever touches a power line, let go of the string at once, keep away, and tell the electricity company for your area.

steps.test: Teach two younger children to launch and land a kite you made, until each of them has done both on their own.
steps.note: Children in your family, a friend's children with their grown-up there, or a group at a club. Show them how to read the wind first, then let them hold the line while you stand beside them. Tell them the power line rule before anything else.
